name: Regression Testing Best Practices
description: This module lists the best, most commonly recommended practices for writing, implementing, and building regression testing — the default, everyday guidance to apply on typical, ordinary regression testing tasks and implementations, not specialized or unusual ones.
content:
This module lists the best, most commonly recommended practices for writing, implementing, and building regression testing — the default, everyday guidance to apply on typical, ordinary regression testing tasks and implementations, not specialized or unusual ones.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. When regression testing decisions are ambiguous, favor the option that is easiest to reverse or extend later.
2. Prefer the simplest regression testing approach that satisfies the requirement over a more general one that isn't needed yet.
3. Check that regression testing terminology is used consistently throughout, matching existing conventions in the surrounding context.
4. Prefer explicit, readable regression testing solutions over clever ones that are hard to verify.
5. Validate regression testing outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
6. Surface known limitations of a chosen regression testing approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
7. Measure before optimizing any regression testing bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.
8. Keep regression testing changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
9. State assumptions about regression testing explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not skip documenting regression testing assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.
- Do not treat a single passing example as full verification of regression testing correctness.
- Do not silently drop regression testing edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for regression testing, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
